questions.prompt: In what order are local variables and class data members destroyed when a scope exits?
options: Alphabetical by identifier name for members, declaration order for locals
Reverse order of construction completion for locals, and reverse declaration order for class members
Forward declaration order so earlier handles close before later ones
Unspecified order unless wrapped inside std::tuple
questions.explanation: Under [basic.stc.auto] and [class.dtor], block-scope objects unwind in exact reverse order of construction completion, while class members are destroyed in reverse order of declaration inside the class definition.

questions.prompt: What is the hidden consequence of adding `~Packet() = default;` to a struct that holds a std::vector<std::byte>?
options: Nothing changes; = default leaves all implicitly generated special members identical
The vector cannot be destroyed unless std::destroy_at is called manually
The struct becomes non-copyable until copy operations are also defaulted
Implicit move constructor and move assignment are suppressed, so moves silently fall back to copying payload
questions.explanation: Under [class.copy.ctor] and [class.copy.assign], any user-declared destructor—even `= default;`—prevents implicit declaration of the move constructor and move assignment operator, turning `std::move(pkt)` into a copy.

questions.prompt: Assume Part(1) succeeds and Part(2) throws std::runtime_error during construction of Assembly. Which destructors run?
options: Only ~Part() for first runs; ~Part() for second and ~Assembly() do NOT run
~Part() for both first and second run, followed by ~Assembly()
Only ~Assembly() runs to clean up both members
No destructors run because the expression failed before Assembly existed
questions.explanation: Under [except.ctor], because Assembly's constructor exited via an exception, Assembly's lifetime never began and ~Assembly() never runs. Every already-completed subobject (here only first) is destroyed immediately.

questions.prompt: Why does `std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>` (with stateless functor `FileCloser`) typically match `sizeof(std::FILE*)`, whereas `std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, int(*)(std::FILE*)>` is larger?
options: std::unique_ptr uses std::shared_ptr's control block whenever a function pointer is passed
Function pointers disable move semantics, forcing std::unique_ptr to allocate a flag
P2 must store the runtime function pointer address inside the smart pointer, while stateless FileCloser takes zero bytes via empty-base / [[no_unique_address]] optimization
FileCloser deletes the pointer at compile time during constexpr evaluation
questions.explanation: A function pointer type `int(*)(std::FILE*)` is stateful runtime data (different pointers share the same type), so unique_ptr must store it. A stateless functor encodes the deleter in the type itself and occupies zero extra bytes.

questions.prompt: What happens in C++23 if a user-declared destructor `~Guard() { cleanup(); }` (with no exception specification) throws an exception at runtime during normal scope exit?
options: The exception propagates normally to the caller's catch block because noexcept was not written
std::terminate() is called because user-declared destructors are implicitly noexcept(true)
The compiler rejects ~Guard() at compile time whenever throw appears inside a destructor
Only throws during stack unwinding terminate; normal scope-exit throws propagate
questions.explanation: Since C++11 ([class.dtor] / [except.spec]), a destructor with no explicit exception specification inherits the exception specification of an implicitly declared destructor—which is `noexcept(true)` unless a base or member destructor can throw. Exiting it via exception calls std::terminate().

questions.prompt: Suppose `Wrapper` declares a custom destructor `~Wrapper() { ... }` and omits copy/move declarations. Why does copying `Wrapper` still compile today despite violating the Rule of Five?
options: Implicit copy operations are forbidden; copying Wrapper only works via memcpy
Move operations are still generated instead of copy operations
User-declared destructors only suppress special members if virtual
Implicit generation of copy constructor and copy assignment is deprecated when a user-declared destructor exists, though still permitted for backward compatibility
questions.explanation: Under [depr.impldec] and [class.copy.ctor], declaring a destructor suppresses implicit move operations outright, whereas implicit copy constructor and copy assignment generation remain allowed—but explicitly deprecated.
